paras: The expulsion of Black residents from Esserville, Virginia, took place in early August 1920, when nearly all of the town's Black population left after an order to 'clear out' that followed the killing of a white policeman named Wilson. Only three Black persons or families were reported to remain, and the town's mayor and the county solicitor appealed without success for the others to return. The episode was reported only in the Black press, which attributed the order variously to the Ku Klux, a band of masked men, or a 'citizens' committee'.

Policeman Wilson, called Tom Wilson by the Chicago Whip and George Wilson by a later Chicago Defender report, was shot dead on a Sunday afternoon in the part of Esserville where Black residents lived. A Bristol dispatch dated August 2 placed the shooting 'last Sunday', which would be about August 1. The accounts agree that he died in a 'pistol duel' with a Black man whose identity was not known and who escaped, according to the Whip, 'to the hills'.

The Defender's correspondent gave a fuller version: Wilson was searching a man arrested for carrying weapons when he was shot in the forehead. Witnesses quoted by the Defender said the officer took a watch and money from the man's pocket and refused to return them, after which the man seized Wilson's revolver and killed him.

In the days after the shooting, an order went out for Black residents to 'clean out at once'. The Baltimore Afro-American, in a dispatch dated August 5, said the order came from 'the local Ku Klux', thought to be friends of the slain officer, and that only three Black persons were permitted to stay. The Defender described the authors of the order as 'a band of masked white men', also said to be Wilson's friends.

The Chicago Whip's Bristol dispatch told it differently, saying the departure followed rumors that all Black people would be driven out and that residents 'took the white hoodlums at their word and left town voluntarily'. According to the Whip, Black residents of the town and surrounding county left behind homes, property, livestock and standing crops, and farm work and domestic service came to a halt.

The mayor and the county solicitor asked Black residents to return and promised them 'full protection', but the Whip reported that none had come back. A Defender follow-up dated August 13 said only three families remained and that northern recruiters had taken more than 200 people to automobile factories in Michigan and Illinois, with others going to Pennsylvania. No report of an arrest of Wilson's killer or of those who issued the order appears in the coverage.

The story ran first in Black weeklies in early August, under headlines that named the attackers: the Afro-American's 'Klu Klux Drive All Other Colored People Out Of The Town of Esserville, Va.' and the Defender's 'DRIVE RACE FROM TOWN AFTER SLAYING'.

The Chicago Whip treated the exodus as a blow to the white town, describing whites who did not 'know how to work' and a 'shiftless element' given to 'pillage and thievery'. On its editorial page the same issue took a different line, asking why the people of 'a certain township in Virginia' had been 'cowardly enough to leave their farms and houses' instead of defending them.

A shorter wire item, which credited the order to a 'citizens' committee' and the killing to 'unknown Negroes', circulated later with fresh datelines. It appeared in the Cleveland Advocate, Kansas City Sun, Phoenix Tribune and Savannah Tribune on August 21 and in the Washington Bee on September 4, the Phoenix Tribune heading it 'Policeman Is Slain By Negro'. No coverage of the episode was found in the white press.

Accounts differ on who drove Black residents out: the Afro-American named the Ku Klux, the Defender a band of masked white men, and the wire brief a citizens' committee. The Whip alone said no order was enforced and that residents left voluntarily on rumors, while the wire brief said Wilson was killed by 'unknown' men rather than a single man.

reader.title: Expulsion of Black residents from Esserville, Virginia
bases: Every account says nearly all Black residents left Esserville after an order or threat to 'clear out' following a white policeman's killing (A1, A2, A4, A8).

Separate Black-press dispatches from Esserville and Bristol and a wire brief agree that Black residents left Esserville after Policeman Wilson's killing, though they differ on who gave the order and whether the departure was forced (A1, A2, A4, A8).

accounts.label: Esserville dispatch to the Afro-American and Defender
accounts.gist: The 'local Ku Klux' or 'a band of masked white men', thought to be friends of the slain policeman, ordered Black residents to 'clean out at once'; only three remained.

accounts.label: Witnesses quoted by the Defender
accounts.gist: Wilson, searching a man arrested for carrying weapons, took his watch and money and refused to return them; the man seized Wilson's revolver, shot him and escaped.

accounts.label: Bristol dispatch in the Chicago Whip
accounts.gist: Black residents left voluntarily on rumors that 'white hoodlums' would drive them out, leaving the town and county without labor; officials asked them to return.

accounts.label: Wire brief
accounts.gist: All but three Black residents were ordered to leave by a 'citizens' committee' after Wilson was killed in the Black quarter by 'unknown Negroes'.

accounts.label: Defender follow-up
accounts.gist: Only three families remained; northern labor agents took more than 200 people to factories after word of an exodus spread.

framing.detail: The Afro-American headlined 'Klu Klux Drive All Other Colored People Out' and the Defender 'DRIVE RACE FROM TOWN AFTER SLAYING', and the Defender printed witnesses who said the officer had robbed the man he shot.
The Chicago Whip described the exodus as a spectacle of white 'pillage and thievery' and 'white hoodlums', while its editor called the departing residents 'cowardly' for leaving their farms.
The wire brief, with its 'citizens' committee' and 'unknown Negroes', ran in several Black weeklies, the Phoenix Tribune under 'Policeman Is Slain By Negro; All Blacks Ordered to Leave City'.

wire brief datelines Aug. 9 to Aug. 19, each repeating 'last Sunday'

conflicts.note: The wire brief was reprinted with fresh datelines; the earliest dispatches (Aug. 2 and Aug. 5) are the better guide to the date. The Whip's 'Yesterday' for the officials' appeal sits awkwardly with an Aug. 2 dateline.
Spelling variants of the same place in the same brief.

record_check.dossier: About 1920-08-01 (killing 'last Sunday' in an Aug. 2 dispatch; order reported by Aug. 5); Aug. 15 is not supported by any report.
Local Ku Klux / masked white men thought to be the officer's friends (A1, A2); a citizens' committee in the wire brief (A8).

record_check.record: Black residents left after rumors that white hoodlums would drive them out
record_check.dossier: Only the Whip gives the voluntary-departure version; other dispatches report an order to clear out from the Ku Klux, masked men or a committee.

info: Policeman Wilson was killed on a Sunday afternoon, which the Aug. 2 dispatch calls 'last Sunday', making it about Aug. 1, 1920; the order and exodus followed within days (reported by Aug. 5).
Esserville, Virginia, in the section of town where Black residents lived; the Whip says the surrounding county was emptied as well.
The Black population of Esserville; all but three persons (A1, A8) or three families (A6) left.
An unidentified Black man was said to have shot and killed Policeman Wilson in a pistol duel and escaped.

Given variously as the 'local Ku Klux' (A1), 'a band of masked white men' (A2), friends of the slain officer (A1, A2, A6), a 'citizens' committee' (A8), or 'white hoodlums' whose rumored threat prompted the departure (A4).

sources.note: Esserville, Aug. 5: 'local Ku Klux' ordered Black people out after a white policeman was killed in a pistol duel 'Sunday afternoon'; only three remained.
quotes: Following an order to clear out at once, given by the local Ku Klux, thought to have been friends of the white policemen who was killed in a pistol-duel by a colored man

sources.note: Esserville, Aug. 6: order to 'clean out at once' from masked white men; witnesses say Officer Wilson took a watch and money from a man he was searching, who seized his revolver and killed him.
quotes: Witnesses declared the officer removed a watch and some money from the man's pocket and refused to return it, whereupon the stranger seized Wilson's revolver and killed him.

sources.note: Bristol, Tenn., Aug. 2: every Black resident left town and county after rumors; Policeman Tom Wilson killed by an unidentified Black man who escaped; mayor and county solicitor asked them to return.
quotes: The wholesale exodus was caused by some rumors that all colored people would be driven from the town. The colored people took the white hoodlums at their word and left town voluntarily
Yesterday the mayor of the town joined with the county solicitor in begging all colored people to return, assuring them full protection.

sources.note: Editorial paragraph: 'a certain township in Virginia' enforced an edict that Black people leave; criticizes them for leaving.
quotes: We wonder why they were cowardly enough to leave their farms and houses of their birthplace.

sources.note: Esserville, Aug. 13 (garbled OCR): only three families remained; over 200 left for northern automobile factories; order followed slaying of 'Officer George Wilson (white)'.
quotes: The order to "clean out" was given when Officer George Wilson (white) was slain in a section of the town occupied by our people.

Esserville, Aug. 19: wire brief; all but three ordered out by a citizens' committee; Wilson killed 'by unknown Negroes'.
